bonus.label: Day-one idea
bonus.title: Not every regulatory change should interrupt someone
bonus.body: Your platform decides which new rules matter to each business. In DR-01 I let severity alone decide whether a notification interrupts or just informs, and kept category cosmetic. I'd start regulatory alerts the same way: one question, does this change require the customer to act before a deadline, decides whether it becomes a task with an owner and a date or a line in a digest. Jurisdiction and topic only shape how it looks. That keeps 'what matters' a product decision you can test, not a side effect of styling.

bonus.label: Onsale idea
bonus.title: An onsale has the same shape as a money order
bonus.body: A money order takes the customer's money for something that hasn't been printed yet, and the printer can fail. A ticket in a high-traffic onsale works the same way: the seat is held, the card is charged, then the ticket is issued, and any step can fail. What I learned at the register carries over. Make each step recover on its own, so a failure releases the hold or refunds the charge without anyone stepping in. And decide up front what the person waiting sees while that happens. I haven't built ticketing, so on day one I'd want to know where your compensating steps live today, and what a fan sees when one runs.

bonus.label: Day-one question
bonus.title: Where a failed print meets a failed load
bonus.body: The hard moment in money orders was a print that failed after the customer had paid. The fix was a saga: the failure triggers its own refund, so nothing is quietly edited and every step stays on the record. I'd expect sterile processing to have the same shape, a load that fails after its sets have moved on and has to be pulled back. My first question would be how SPM models that reversal: as edits to the original records, or as its own recall step with its own trail. If it's the first, that's where I'd want to start.
